title: Predicting relationships from data and processes
blurb: Read a table, graph or process and predict what happens next: direct, inverse, peaked, leveling-off and doubling patterns, and body cause-and-effect chains.
question: A lab table shows a bacterial culture doubling every 20 minutes, and a graph shows gas pressure falling as volume rises. How many bacteria will there be after 2 hours, what happens to the gas pressure if the volume is halved, and how far can you trust each prediction?

teach.body: Formally, predicting a relationship means identifying how a dependent variable responds to changes in an independent variable or to a step in a process, then applying that pattern to a new case. In plain English: spot the pattern (up together, one up and one down, a peak, a leveling off, a doubling) and follow it one step further. The answer must follow from the data or process given, not from a fact you happen to know.

teach.caption: Other inverse examples: as altitude rises, air pressure and the boiling point of water fall.

teach.h: Direct and inverse on one graph
teach.caption: Direct: double x and y doubles. Inverse (like pressure and volume at constant temperature): double x and y halves.

teach.h: Interpolate with confidence, extrapolate with care
teach.body: Interpolation estimates a value BETWEEN measured data points, and it is fairly reliable. Extrapolation predicts BEYOND the range tested, and it is risky: a trend may level off, peak or reverse outside the data. If a drug was tested from 10 to 40 mg, predicting 25 mg is interpolation; predicting 80 mg is extrapolation.

teach.caption: Follow each arrow one step at a time; a reversed step (ADH falls) is the classic wrong option.

teach.body: Malik, a nursing applicant in a microbiology lab, starts a culture of 100 bacteria that double every 20 minutes. Two hours is 120 ÷ 20 = 6 generations. Cells = 100 x 2⁶ = 100 x 64 = 6,400. A linear guess (adding 100 each time) would give only 700. He should not extrapolate to 24 hours, though: nutrients run out, and real growth levels off.

teach.text: Classic errors: assuming a trend continues forever (extrapolation); reading the independent variable as the outcome; calling a downward slope 'direct'; predicting linear growth when it is exponential; and choosing an option that is a true fact but does not follow from the scenario given.

items: Direct: both rise together. Inverse: one rises as the other falls. None: random scatter.
Nonlinear: plateau (saturation), peak (optimum), exponential growth (2ⁿ) and decay (half-life).
Interpolation (between points) is more reliable than extrapolation (beyond the range).
Dehydration: osmolality up, ADH up, less and darker urine.
Blood loss: BP down, heart rate up, vasoconstriction. Exercise: CO₂ up, breathing up.
A catalyst speeds a reaction without changing the products.

summary: You can now classify a relationship as direct, inverse, none or nonlinear from a table or graph, and predict the next value, including exponential doubling. You can also follow body and chemical cause-and-effect chains and judge when a prediction stretches beyond the data.

A.q: A sealed syringe of gas is kept at constant temperature. The plunger is pushed in until the gas volume is halved. What happens to the gas pressure?
options: It halves
It stays the same
It doubles
It increases fourfold
A.why: At constant temperature, gas pressure and volume are inversely related: halving the volume doubles the pressure.

whyNot.0: Halving the pressure along with the volume would be a direct relationship; pressure and volume are inverse.
whyNot.1: Pressure and volume are inversely related, so changing the volume must change the pressure.
whyNot.3: This overshoots: an inverse relationship means halving one doubles the other, not quadruples it.

A.q: After a large meal, a person's blood glucose rises. Which response is predicted?
options: Insulin rises, then blood glucose falls
Glucagon rises, then blood glucose falls
Insulin falls, then blood glucose rises
Glucagon falls, then blood glucose rises
A.why: High blood glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers blood glucose back toward normal (negative feedback).

whyNot.1: Glucagon raises blood glucose; it is released when glucose is LOW.
whyNot.2: Insulin rises, not falls, when glucose is high, and the feedback brings glucose down.
whyNot.3: This predicts glucose rising further, the opposite of the feedback response.

A.q: A student records the boiling point of water at four altitudes: 0 m, 100 °C; 1,000 m, 97 °C; 2,000 m, 93 °C; 3,000 m, 90 °C. Which describes the relationship?
options: Direct: boiling point rises as altitude rises
Direct: boiling point falls as altitude rises
No relationship: the values are scattered randomly
Inverse: boiling point falls as altitude rises
A.why: As one variable (altitude) increases, the other (boiling point) decreases steadily: an inverse relationship.

whyNot.0: The boiling point falls in the data; it does not rise.
whyNot.1: The description is right but the label is wrong: one rising while the other falls is inverse, not direct.
whyNot.2: The values change steadily in one direction, which is a clear trend, not random scatter.

B.q: A runner becomes dehydrated during a long race. Which changes are predicted?
options: ADH falls; less urine, darker in color
ADH rises; less urine, darker in color
ADH rises; more urine, lighter in color
ADH falls; more urine, lighter in color
B.why: Dehydration raises plasma osmolality, which increases ADH. ADH makes the kidneys conserve water, so urine is reduced and more concentrated (darker).

whyNot.0: The urine change is right, but ADH rises, not falls, when the body is short of water.
whyNot.2: ADH does rise, but its effect is to reduce urine output, not increase it.
whyNot.3: Falling ADH and more dilute urine is the response to too much water, not dehydration.

B.q: A drug's effect on heart rate was measured at doses of 10, 20, 30 and 40 mg. Which prediction is the MOST reliable?
options: The effect at a 25 mg dose
The effect at an 80 mg dose
The effect at a 2 mg dose
The effect after 10 years of daily use
B.why: 25 mg lies between tested doses, so the prediction is an interpolation, which is more reliable than going beyond the data.

whyNot.1: 80 mg is double the highest dose tested: an extrapolation, where the trend may change.
whyNot.2: 2 mg lies below the lowest dose tested, so it is also an extrapolation.
whyNot.3: Long-term effects lie far outside the time range studied: an extrapolation.

B.q: A catalyst is added to a slow chemical reaction. Which outcome is predicted?
options: Faster rate, different products
Slower rate, more product formed
Faster rate, same products
Same rate, larger amount of product
B.why: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up and without changing what the products are.

whyNot.0: The rate does increase, but a catalyst does not change the products.
whyNot.1: A catalyst speeds a reaction up; it does not slow it down.
whyNot.3: The catalyst's effect is on the rate, not on the amount of product.

C.q: An enzyme's reaction rate is measured at five temperatures: 20 °C, 12 units; 30 °C, 25 units; 40 °C, 38 units; 50 °C, 20 units; 60 °C, 4 units. Which statement BEST describes the relationship?
options: Rate rises steadily with temperature
Rate falls steadily with temperature
Rate rises, then levels off
Rate rises to a peak, then falls
C.why: The rate climbs to a maximum at 40 °C (the optimum among those tested) and then drops: a rise-then-fall pattern.

whyNot.0: The rate falls above 40 °C, so the rise is not steady across the range.
whyNot.1: The rate rises from 20 °C to 40 °C before it falls.
whyNot.2: Leveling off would keep the rate near its maximum; here it drops sharply to 4 units.

C.q: A culture of 500 bacteria doubles every 20 minutes. Assuming conditions stay ideal, how many bacteria are present after 2 hours?

whyNot.0: This multiplies 500 by 6, treating exponential growth as linear.

C.q: A patient loses a large volume of blood after an injury. Which set of changes is predicted?
options: BP falls; heart rate rises; vessels constrict
BP falls; heart rate falls; vessels dilate
BP rises; heart rate rises; vessels constrict
BP rises; heart rate falls; vessels dilate
C.why: Less blood volume lowers blood pressure; the body compensates by raising heart rate and constricting vessels.

whyNot.1: A falling heart rate and dilated vessels would lower blood pressure further, the opposite of compensation.
whyNot.2: The compensations are right, but the starting change is a FALL in blood pressure.
whyNot.3: Blood loss lowers, not raises, blood pressure, and the compensations are reversed.

reteach.title: Rumors and seesaws
reteach.question: How do a seesaw and a rumor spreading through a school help you predict inverse and exponential relationships?

blocks.body: A seesaw is an inverse relationship: when one end goes up, the other goes down. Pressure and volume of a trapped gas behave the same way. A rumor is exponential: you tell 2 friends, each tells 2 more, and the number hearing it each round goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, doubling each round, which grows far faster than adding 2 each time. But a rumor stops spreading once everyone at school has heard it: that is why extrapolating a trend far past the data is risky.

blocks.caption: Both start from 1. Doubling soon leaves adding far behind.

blocks.text: Real limits bend every curve: a rumor runs out of listeners, bacteria run out of food, and an enzyme runs out of substrate or is damaged by heat. Predict within the data first.

explain.body: Direct: both variables increase together (upward slope). Inverse: one increases as the other decreases (downward slope). No relationship: random scatter.

test.q: As the temperature of the gas in a flexible balloon (at constant pressure) rises, the balloon's volume increases. This is:
options: An inverse relationship
A direct relationship
A random scatter
An exponential decay
test.why: Volume increases as temperature increases: both rise together, a direct relationship.

whyNot.0: In an inverse relationship one variable falls as the other rises; here both rise.
whyNot.2: The volume changes consistently with temperature, so the data are not random.
whyNot.3: Exponential decay halves at each step; here the volume grows.

explain.body: Some relationships curve: rise then plateau (saturation), rise then fall (optimum), exponential growth (doubling, 2ⁿ) and exponential decay (halving, half-life).

test.q: A single bacterium divides by binary fission. Assuming every cell divides each generation, how many cells are there after 5 generations?

whyNot.0: This multiplies 2 by 5 (linear growth) instead of doubling 5 times (2⁵).
whyNot.2: This is 5², squaring the generation number instead of doubling each time.

explain.body: Interpolation estimates between measured points and is fairly reliable. Extrapolation predicts beyond the tested range and is risky, because trends can level off, peak or reverse.

options: Estimating between measured data points
Predicting beyond the range of the data
Repeating trials to confirm the data
Plotting the dependent variable on y
test.why: Extrapolation extends a trend beyond the range actually measured.

whyNot.0: Estimating between measured points is interpolation.
whyNot.2: Repeating trials is replication, which improves reliability.
whyNot.3: Placing the dependent variable on the y-axis is a graphing convention, not a prediction method.

explain.body: Follow a process one link at a time: exercise raises CO₂, which raises breathing rate; blood loss lowers BP, which raises heart rate; dehydration raises ADH, which reduces urine output.

test.q: During hard exercise, muscles produce more carbon dioxide. What change in breathing is predicted?
options: Breathing rate slows down
Breathing rate is unchanged
Breathing rate speeds up
Breathing pauses briefly
test.why: Rising CO₂ is detected and breathing rate increases to remove the extra CO₂.

whyNot.0: Slower breathing would let CO₂ build up further.
whyNot.1: The body responds to higher CO₂; breathing does not stay the same.
whyNot.3: Pausing breathing would raise CO₂ even more; the response is faster breathing.
